title: Still open
hook: the questions this year didn't close
carry: a door you know the location of

segments.voice: Yesterday, Meditations, and your line was what changed: the old page on death, and the new lines written beside it. Some things moved. Today is for the things that didn't settle at all. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

Plenty of kitchens have one drawer for things that don't belong anywhere else. Rubber bands, a key nobody can identify, the instructions for something you no longer own. You don't throw the drawer out. You just know it's there. A year of great questions has a drawer like that too. Suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe: some of what we asked got an answer you could hold. And some of it got a stack of answers that don't agree, or no answer at all. Today we open the drawer, on purpose, and leave it open.
screen: `A DRAWER FOR WHAT DOESN'T FIT.` → `SOME QUESTIONS DIDN'T SETTLE.` → `OPEN THE DRAWER.`

segments.voice: First, the question even the gods doubted. In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa finds himself at the house of Death, and asks what happens to a person after dying: some say he is, some say he is not. Death answers that even the gods were once in doubt about this, that it's subtle and hard to know, and offers him wealth, long life and land if he'll ask anything else. Nachiketa keeps his question. Some questions are worth more than every prize offered for dropping them. Second, the hymn that wonders. The Hymn of Creation in the Rig Veda asks how everything began, and ends by wondering whether even the one who watches from the highest heaven knows, or perhaps does not know. A sacred text that leaves its own question open. Third, the brother who won't sign. In Dostoevsky's The Brothers Karamazov, Ivan says he can't accept a final harmony bought with a child's suffering. His brother Alyosha, who believes, answers from his own faith, but he doesn't walk away, and the chapter doesn't settle it for either of them. The novel keeps them both at the table. Fourth, open is not empty. These traditions have answers, and people live whole lives inside them. On this path, the answers stay in their own homes, and the choosing stays with you. So a question still open at the end of the year isn't a gap in the work. It's a door you know the location of. Some people keep a short list of questions like this and look at it once a year. Not to close them. To see which ones have changed shape, which ones have gone quiet, and which ones still wake them at night.
screen: `NACHIKETA KEEPS HIS QUESTION.` · `THE HYMN THAT WONDERS IF ANYONE KNOWS.` · `IVAN WON'T SIGN.` · `OPEN IS NOT EMPTY.` · then, large: `STILL OPEN.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is a list. Sit, and let the year's six questions pass by one at a time: suffering, death, love, work, forgiveness, awe. Don't hurry. As each one passes, notice whether something in it still tugs. A why. A what if. A person you still can't make sense of. After the bell, write down the questions that are still open for you, as plainly as you can, one per line. Three is plenty. If you pray, you can bring the list into prayer. If you don't, just keep it somewhere you'll find it again. The bell holds the time.
Still open. The questions this year asked and didn't close: kept, named, and left on purpose with the door ajar. Today's word.

Your line: a door you know the location of. When one of your open questions comes up today, don't rush to settle it. Say to yourself, a door you know the location of, and let it stay. Day one thousand fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Some people on many paths keep a written list of their unanswered questions and return to it at the end of a year, noticing which ones have changed rather than trying to close them.

trapdoor: what you thought: an open question is one nobody bothered to answer.
what it means: a question kept open on purpose, after you've heard the answers and they didn't agree.
what a scholar hears: the Rig Veda's Hymn of Creation closes on 'perhaps he does not know', and in the Katha Upanishad Death himself admits the gods once doubted the boy's question.
